title: The Operators
dek: The mechanics of outsized agency, studied at the extremes, stripped from the cruelty, and pointed at building rather than conquering.

entries.h: To understand a trait, study where it is most exaggerated
p: The most ambitious people in history are the far tail of the agency distribution, which is where the mechanics become impossible to miss. That is the entire justification for studying them, and it comes with a condition I want stated before anything else.

entries.h: Steal the engine. Refuse the cruelty
p: Most of these figures were ruthless and many caused staggering harm — wars, conquest, exploitation, monopoly abuse. I am not interested in admiring that and I am not going to pretend the achievements cancel it.

The engine — obsession, speed, audacity, energy, the refusal of inherited constraints, the ability to attract talent — is separable from the aim. The same engine inside a good compass is how most good things got built; with no compass it is how the worst things happened. The difference is entirely the steering, and the steering is a choice.

entries.h: Six traits that keep recurring across centuries
p: Obsession. A bias to action and speed. Audacity. Relentless energy. A refusal to accept constraints as given. And a magnetism for talent.

None is a fixed endowment. Obsession follows from finding the right problem; speed and audacity are habits you rep; energy is built on the substrate from Manual I. But the engine has a required ignition, and it is action — because anything multiplied by zero is zero.

entries.h: Whoever cycles the loop faster wins
p: John Boyd's OODA loop — observe, orient, decide, act — carries an insight beyond air combat: the winner is usually not the biggest brain but the fastest loop, because each completed cycle produces real feedback that sharpens the next one. Speed compounds.

The reason to act before feeling ready is not recklessness. It is that action is how you observe at all. You cannot orient on a situation you have never touched, and planners stay on Observe indefinitely.

entries.h: About seventy per cent of the information you wish you had
p: Waiting for ninety per cent means being slow, and slow is usually the more expensive error. Pair this with regret-minimisation for the genuinely large calls — imagine yourself at eighty looking back, and notice that the timid option almost never wins that comparison.
And apply the asymmetry from Manual I: when the downside is capped and the upside is not, hesitation is the expensive choice.

Napoleon: out-prepare everyone, then commit totally and fast. He was not a reckless genius; he mapped logistics, terrain and the opponent's psychology in advance, and only then moved without hesitation. Reject: the wars.

Rockefeller: temperament and compounding beat flash. Disciplined, calm, long-horizon, obsessed with systems and reinvestment. Reject: the predatory monopoly, which was not strategy but a crime that paid for a while.
Caesar and Alexander: at the rare genuinely irreversible moment, half-measures lose. Recognise the hinge and pour everything into it. Reject: conquest as the goal.
The builders: today's founders run the identical software aimed at building rather than conquering — which is the proof the engine does not require a body count.

entries.h: Power corrodes the compass, so make the correction structural
p: Do not rely on remaining a good person by intention. Keep people close who will tell you the truth to your face and are not dependent on you, and tie the ambition to making the pie bigger rather than enlarging your slice.
The whole of this manual in one sentence: the operator's engine inside a good person's compass. Rare precisely because most people get one or the other.

heur.s: Reading and planning are both Observe. The loop does not turn until you act.

heur.b: Do I have seventy per cent?
heur.s: Then go. Ninety per cent is a story you tell yourself about being careful.

heur.b: Is this a hinge or a two-way door?
heur.s: Total commitment at the hinge; speed everywhere else.

heur.b: Who around me will actually tell me I am wrong?
heur.s: If the honest answer is nobody, that is the emergency.
